Exploratory time series analysis
text:
Visualising temporal patterns
Creating a time plot with autoplot() is quick and easy. A time plot can also be made with the grammar of time series graphics for more options.

pbs_scripts |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Month, y = Scripts)) +
  geom_time_line()

title: Exploratory time series analysis
text:
Time scales
Axis breaks use durations, and labels use calendar components.

pbs_scripts |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Month, y = Scripts)) +
  geom_time_line() +
  scale_x_mixtime(
    time_breaks = years(2L),
    time_labels = "{lin(year)}"
  )








lin() is linear and cyc() is cyclical time.

title: Exploratory time series analysis
text:
Visualising temporal patterns
The time plot allows us identify the presence of seasonality, but it is less effective in seeing the shape of seasonal patterns.







Question


How else could we represent time to more clearly show annual seasonal patterns?

title: Exploratory time series analysis
text:
Visualising seasonality
Looping the plot’s x-axis around each year arranges linear time (year month) cyclically (month of year), which highlights seasonal patterns.






Exercise 8


Loop the time axis of this plot with coord_loop().

pbs_scripts |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Month, y = Scripts)) +
  geom_time_line() +
  coord_loop(time_loops = ???)

Hint: time_loops is a mixtime duration, such as weeks(2L) for a fortnight.

title: Exploratory time series analysis
text:
Visualising seasonality

pbs_scripts |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Month, y = Scripts)) +
  geom_time_line() +
  coord_loop(time_loops = years(1L))

title: Exploratory time series analysis
text:
How looping works








Monthly scripts in linear time.


Each month belongs to a year. Split the line between years.


Loop each year back to the start, one at a time.


The season plot: cyclical time.
December still connects to the next January.

title: Exploratory time series analysis
text:
Why loop time?
Without coord_loop(), the season plot needs seasonal factors.

aes(
  x = lubridate::month(Month, label = TRUE),
  group = lubridate::year(Month)
)







Seasonal factors are error-prone



the wrong group draws sawtooth lines
December isn’t connected to January
each month has equal length
x and group both change with the season

title: Exploratory time series analysis
text:
Circular time
Looped time can also be drawn around a circle.

pbs_scripts |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Month, y = Scripts)) +
  geom_time_line() +
  coord_loop(
    time_loops = years(1L),
    coord = coord_radial()
  )

title: Exploratory time series analysis
text:
The season plot

pbs_scripts |>
  gg_season(Scripts, period = years(1L))








This plot is known as a season plot, which can be made quickly with the plot helper function gg_season().

title: Exploratory time series analysis
text:
The seasonal period

pbs_scripts |>
  gg_season(Scripts, period = years(1L))

The period argument is a duration for the length of the data’s seasonal pattern.
It uses coord_loop(time_loops = period), so that the time axis loops around each year.
Other common seasonal periods include:

weeks(1L)
days(1L)
hours(1L)

title: Exploratory time series analysis
text:
Visualising seasonality

aus_production |>
  gg_season(Gas, period = years(1L))















Describing the seasonal pattern


This plot shows that peak production is in Q3 with a trough in Q1. Seasonality is getting stronger recently.











Can we do better?


It’s hard to see the seasonality from the early data, how can we improve it?

title: Exploratory time series analysis
text:
Visualising seasonality


aus_production |>
  gg_season(log(Gas), period = years(1L))











aus_production |>
  gg_season(Gas, period = years(1L)) +
  scale_y_log10()















Plotting log transformed data


Recall that log transforming the data rescales multiplicative patterns into additive ones.












Can we do better?


The trend makes it difficult to compare across and within seasons, can we remove the trend?

title: Exploratory time series analysis
Exploratory time series analysis
text:
Visualising seasonality







Remap the aesthetics


Swap the x and colour aesthetic mappings to plot linear time on the x-axis, with colours for each quarter.




aus_production |>
  model(STL(log(Gas))) |>
  components() |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = Quarter,
    y = season_year,
    colour =
      format(Quarter, "Q{cyc(quarter, year)}")
  )) +
  geom_time_line() +
  labs(
    x = "Time",
    y = "Seasonality",
    colour = "Quarter",
    title = "Gas production in Australia"
  )


















Gas production in Q1 is increasing while Q3 is decreasing.

title: Exploratory time series analysis
text:
From time plot to subseries plot








The seasonal component of log gas production.


Each observation belongs to a quarter.


Join observations from the same quarter: four subseries.


Place the subseries side by side to compare quarters.


Add the mean of each quarter: the seasonal subseries plot.

The seasonal subseries plot

aus_production |>
  gg_subseries(Gas, period = years(1L))








This plot is known as a seasonal subseries plot, which can be made quickly with the plot helper function gg_subseries().

title: Exploratory time series analysis
text:
Complex seasonality
Complex seasonality describes two or more seasonal patterns.
Complex seasonal patterns:

often interact with each-other
can be based on other calendars (e.g. holidays)








Frequent seasonality


Multiple seasonality is common in daily & sub-daily data.
It can be difficult to forecast, so first consider if you need daily or sub-daily forecasts for making decisions.

title: Exploratory time series analysis
text:
Complex seasonality
There are three key strategies for clearly plotting multiple seasonal patterns:







Temporal aggregation


Sum over finer-grained seasonal patterns.
Useful for annual seasonality.











Calendar plots


Lay out time like a calendar.
Useful for holidays and sub-daily patterns.











Seasonal decomposition


Separate each seasonal pattern with MSTL (multiple STL).
Best for daily / weekly seasonality.

Temporal aggregation
The Victorian electricity demand data has three seasonal patterns:

Annual (weather)
Weekly (work)
Daily (sleep)

2 2012-01-01 00:30 AEDT  4263.        21.0 TRUE   
3 2012-01-01 01:00 AEDT  4049.        20.7 TRUE

Temporal aggregation
When plotted at a 30 minute frequency, it is difficult to see any seasonal pattern clearly.

vic_elec |>

title: Exploratory time series analysis
Exploratory time series analysis
Exploratory time series analysis
text:
Temporal aggregation
stat_summary_time() aggregates within the plot.

vic_daily |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Day, y = Demand)) +
  geom_time_line(colour = "grey60") +
  stat_summary_time(
    granule = weeks(1L), fun = mean,
    colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 1
  )








Incomplete weeks become NA.

title: Exploratory time series analysis
text:
Temporal aggregation

vic_weekly |>
  gg_season(
    Demand,
    period = years(1L, calendar = cal_isoweek)
  )














Which year?


Weeks can span two Gregorian years, so they loop around the ISO week calendar’s years.

text:
Time zones
Local time repeats when daylight saving ends.

x <- datetime(
  "2026-04-05 01:30:00",
  tz = "Australia/Melbourne"
)
x + hours(1:2)

<mixtime[2]>
[1] 2026-04-05 02:30:00 AEDT 2026-04-05 02:30:00 AEST



A day isn’t always 24 hours!

x + days(1L)

<mixtime[1]>
[1] 2026-04-06 01:30:00 AEST

x + hours(24L)

<mixtime[1]>
[1] 2026-04-06 00:30:00 AEST

title: Exploratory time series analysis
text:
Absolute and local time
Sub-daily time is shown in absolute time.

dst <- vic_elec |>
  filter(
    date(Time) >= date("2012-03-31"),
    date(Time) <= date("2012-04-02")
  )
dst |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Time, y = Demand)) +
  geom_time_line() +
  scale_x_mixtime(time_breaks = days(1L))








Daylight saving ended at 3am on 1 April 2012.

title: Exploratory time series analysis
text:
Absolute and local time

Use tz = NA for local time, changes are dashed.


dst |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Time, y = Demand)) +
  geom_time_line() +
  scale_x_mixtime(
    time_breaks = days(1L),
    time_chronon =
      cal_gregorian$minute(30L, tz = NA)
  )









Local time aligns human behaviour, absolute time shows when events coincide.

title: Exploratory time series analysis
text:
Seasonal decomposition
Specific combinations of seasonal patterns can also be computed and plotted.


dcmp |>
  gg_season(
    season_day + season_week, period = weeks(1L)
  )
















Caution: model limitations


Recall the STL decomposition is additive, so interactions between different seasonality will not be captured. The seasonal components are only as accurate as the model.

CautionExercise 2



Identify the index and key variables of the aus_accommodation dataset.
Then use as_tsibble() to convert it into a tsibble.

read.csv(
  "https://workshop.nectric.com.au/wombat2026/data/aus_accommodation.csv"
)






NoteSolution





The index is Date and the key is State. Date is read as text, so parse it first.
accommodation <- read.csv(
  "https://workshop.nectric.com.au/wombat2026/data/aus_accommodation.csv"
)
accommodation |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(Date = as.Date(Date)) |>
  as_tsibble(index = Date, key = State)

Exploratory time series analysis
text:
Course Overview
Modern time-series datasets are hard to explore: they contain a large number of frequently observed series, each with many patterns of its own. This workshop introduces exploratory techniques to uncover meaningful temporal patterns in time series data.
Time series data can be tricky to represent correctly, especially when the data spans multiple timezones and granularities. The correct representation of time is essential for accurate analysis, and we’ll see how to avoid common errors in mixed-granularity operations such as temporal aggregation.
Next we’ll explore how to compare patterns across many series using feature-based statistical summaries. Visualising these features reveals common temporal patterns at scale, allowing us to quantify and cluster the dynamics of entire collections of time series.
Finally we’ll visually explore individual time series in detail, using simple plot helpers to quickly create charts that highlight common time series patterns. We’ll also leverage the flexibility of the grammar of time series graphics to uncover more complex patterns, such as visualising seasonality across time zones and using calendar plots to reveal holiday effects.
This practical workshop features live demonstrations and hands-on exercises using real-world data, built around tidy time series tools that extend the tidyverse and ggplot2: feasts, and the new packages mixtime and ggtime. Participants will leave with practical skills to accurately explore and visualise time series data in R.
This workshop will run in-person at WOMBAT 2026 in Melbourne, Australia on November 30th 2026, from 1:30pm to 5:00pm (3 hours of content with a 30 minute break).

title: Exploratory time series analysis
text:
Learning objectives
Participants will learn how to:

Use the tidyverse to wrangle and manipulate time series data
Visualise data and identify common time series patterns
Use time series features to find patterns in many time series
Apply the grammar of time series graphics to visualise complex seasonalities

Instructor
 Mitchell O’Hara-Wild (he/him) is a PhD candidate at Monash University, creating new techniques and tools for forecasting large collections of time series with Rob Hyndman and George Athanasopoulos. He is the lead developer of the tidy time-series forecasting tools fable and feasts, and has co-developed the widely used forecast package since 2015. He is an award-winning educator, and has taught applied forecasting at Monash University and various forecasting workshops around the world.

Required software
To be able to complete the exercises of this workshop, please install a suitable IDE (such as RStudio), a recent version of R (4.1+), and the packages fpp3, feasts, mixtime, and ggtime, which can all be installed with the code below.
install.packages(c("fpp3", "feasts", "mixtime", "ggtime"))
If you installed these packages before the workshop week, please run this again to get the latest versions.
Please have the required software installed before attending the workshop.






NoteOptional: development versions





Some workshop examples use features newer than the CRAN releases. The slides can still be followed with the CRAN versions, but these examples may differ or error:

stat_summary_time() and the axis style used in the slides need the development version of ggtime.
Seasonal peaks and level shifts shown as times (rather than integers) need the development version of feasts.

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak(c("tidyverts/feasts", "mitchelloharawild/ggtime"))

The tsibble data format

A tsibble is a tibble for time series!
The quarterly visitors to Australia are found in the tourism dataset.

Visualising time series
Time series visualisation helps us identify time series patterns.

  geom_time_line(colour = "grey60") +

Lag plots
A lag plot compares observations with those before them, coloured by season.

aus_production |>
  gg_lag(Gas, geom = "point", period = years(1L))

title: Exploratory time series analysis
text:
From lag plots to the ACF








Quarterly Australian beer production since 1992.


Shift a copy (blue) by one quarter, pairing each observation with the one before it.


Each pair is a point in the lag plot. The first observation has no pair.


The autocorrelation \(r_1\) is the linear relationship in this lag plot (blue line).
It is small and negative: the first bar.


At lag 2, quarters are paired with those half a year earlier.
Peaks meet troughs, so \(r_2\) is strongly negative.


At lag 3, quarters are paired with the next quarter of the previous year.
Like lag 1, these are neighbouring quarters.


At lag 4, quarters are paired with the same quarter a year earlier.
Peaks meet peaks, so \(r_4\) is large and positive.


Continue for lags 5, 6, …
The seasonal lags 8, 12 and 16 are strongly positive too.


The ACF plot: one bar for each lag plot.
Bars beyond the dashed lines are unlikely for uncorrelated data.

title: Exploratory time series analysis
text:
Time series decomposition
Decomposition separates time series patterns into individual series.






Additive decomposition via STL


\[y_t = S_t + T_t + R_t\]

\(y_t=\) data at time \(t\)
\(T_t=\) trend-cycle component at time \(t\)
\(S_t=\) seasonal component at time \(t\)
\(R_t=\) remainder component at time \(t\)

title: Exploratory time series analysis
text:
Additive & multiplicative patterns
STL only works with additive patterns
\[y_t = S_t + T_t + R_t\]


Code
library(ggplot2)

i <- 1:119
pattern_types_demo <- tsibble(
  time = yearmonth("2000 Jan") + i,
  season = sin(i*2*pi/12),
  trend = i,
  remainder = rnorm(length(i)),
  index = time
)
pattern_types_demo |> 
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(season, trend, remainder)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = time, y = value, group = name)) +
  geom_time_line() +
  facet_grid(vars(name), scales = "free_y") + 
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)

title: Exploratory time series analysis
text:
Additive & multiplicative patterns
\[y_t = S_t + T_t + R_t\]


Code
pattern_types_demo |>
  autoplot(trend + 10*season + 3*remainder)

title: Exploratory time series analysis
text:
Additive & multiplicative patterns
\[y_t = S_t \times T_t \times R_t\]


Code
pattern_types_demo |>
  autoplot((2 + season) * trend * (5 + remainder))

text:
Additive or multiplicative?














Total retail turnover: additive or multiplicative patterns?


Additive
Multiplicative

title: Exploratory time series analysis
text:
Additive or multiplicative?
















Multiplicative!


STL won’t accurately decompose the patterns in this data.

title: Exploratory time series analysis
text:
STL for multiplicative patterns
While STL doesn’t work directly with multiplicative patterns, we have a transformational trick 🪄

\[\begin{align}
y_t &= S_t \times T_t \times R_t\\
\log(y_t) &= \log\left(S_t \times T_t \times R_t\right)\log\\
&= \log(S_t) + \log(T_t) + \log(R_t)
\end{align}\]








Other transformations


Multiplicative patterns aren’t always exactly multiplicative. Instead we often use power transformations via box_cox(y, lambda).
More info: https://otexts.com/fpp3/transformations.html

Time series features

The signal to noise ratio of seasonality from 0-1.
